content: Hagenia abyssinica is a species of flowering plant that is indigenous to the high-altitude Afro-montane regions of central and eastern Africa. Its distribution is disjunct, occurring in the high mountains of East Africa, ranging from Sudan and Ethiopia in the north, through Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Tanzania, and extending to Malawi and Zambia in the south. In English, it is commonly referred to as African redwood, brayera, cusso, hagenia, or kousso. In Amharic, it is known as kosso, and in Swahili, it is called mdobore or mloziloz. Hagenia abyssinica is the only species within the genus Hagenia, and its closest botanical relative is the Afro-montane genus Leucosidea. Synonyms for this species include Banksia abyssinica, Brayera anthelmintica, Hagenia abyssinica var. viridifolia, and Hagenia anthelmintica. This tree is slender and can grow up to 20 meters in height. It has a short trunk, thick branches, and bark that is thick and peels off. The leaves are compound, reaching up to 40 cm in length, and consist of 7 to 13 leaflets. Each leaflet is approximately 10 cm long, with finely serrated edges, green on the upper surface, and silvery-haired on the underside. The flowers are produced in panicles that are 30 to 60 cm long and range in color from white to orange-buff or pinkish-red. Hagenia abyssinica typically grows at elevations between 2000 and 3000 meters in areas that receive annual rainfall of 1000 to 1500 mm. It is found in mixed Afro-montane forests alongside species such as Podocarpus and Afrocarpus, as well as in drier Afro-montane forests and woodlands where it may dominate or grow in mixed stands with Juniperus procera. Additionally, it serves as a food source for the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species, including the Turnip Moth. Medicinal Uses Kosso, also known as kousso or cusso, is a medicinal preparation derived from the panicles of the pistillate flowers of Hagenia abyssinica. Historically, during the time of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, the drug was imported in the form of cylindrical rolls approximately 18 inches in length and 2 inches in diameter. These rolls contained the entire inflorescence or panicle, which was kept intact by a transverse band wound around it. The active compound in kosso is koussin (or kosin), with the chemical formula C31H33O10. This substance is soluble in alcohol and alkalis and is typically administered in doses of two grams. Kosso is also used as an unstrained infusion made from coarsely powdered flowers, which are ingested along with the liquid. It is considered an effective anthelmintic, particularly for treating infections caused by the pork tapeworm (Taenia solium). Its anthelmintic properties are similar to those of Male Fern (Dryopteris filix-mas). The use of kosso as a treatment was adopted from Ethiopia, where it played a significant role in traditional medicine. Richard Pankhurst, citing Merab, noted that kosso accounted for a substantial portion of Ethiopia's pharmacopoeia. Its primary use, well into the 19th century, was to combat human tapeworm infestations, which were endemic due to the widespread consumption of raw beef dishes such as kitfo and gored gored. Frequent administration of kosso, approximately once every two months, was a common practice for treating tapeworm infections. Pankhurst documented numerous examples of this practice, highlighting that the bi-monthly kosso treatment often became a significant event for the patient. During this time, individuals would withdraw from normal activities, and the phrase the master has taken his kosso became synonymous with being unavailable. Kosso consumption was even used as an excuse to avoid appointments, delay court appearances, or postpone responding to official summonses. In Amharic, the term kosso (ኮሶ) also refers to the human tapeworm, Taenia saginata. However, treatment with Hagenia abyssinica is often only partially effective, frequently resulting in incomplete removal of the intestinal parasite.
